historical_timeline.summary: First neurological symptoms; batting average fell to .295.
Took himself out of the lineup after 2,130 consecutive games.
Diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis certified at the Mayo Clinic.
Retired from baseball on Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day.
Accepted appointment as a New York City Parole Commissioner.
Died at home in the Bronx.
Published discussion of the head-trauma hypothesis and the sealed records.

claims.statement: Henry Louis Gehrig was born on June 19, 1903, in the Yorkville section of Manhattan, New York, to Heinrich and Christina Gehrig, German immigrants.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The birth date used for the synthetic date of birth.

claims.statement: Three of his siblings died young: his sister Anna in September 1902 at about three months, his sister Sophie in the winter of 1906 of a combination of measles, diphtheria and bronchopneumonia, and a brother shortly after birth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history; the causes of Anna's and the infant brother's deaths are not recorded in the cited source.

claims.statement: He enrolled at Columbia University on a football scholarship in February 1921.
He played first base for the New York Yankees and, on May 2, 1939, in Detroit, took himself out of the lineup after a then-record 2,130 consecutive games.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the index date. PBS gives May 1, 1939; the Hall of Fame and SABR accounts of Detroit on May 2 are used.

claims.statement: In 1938 he batted .295, the first time under .300 since 1925, and his hitting fell off sharply in midsummer; he had an attack of lumbago and a badly jammed thumb that season. In the winter of 1938 to 1939 he lost his strength and collapsed while ice skating, in spring training 1939 he collapsed while putting on his uniform pants and his reflexes had slowed alarmingly, and at 35 he batted .143 in the first games of the 1939 season.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern presenting problem: a year of progressive weakness and loss of coordination.

claims.statement: His first neurological symptoms began in 1938, around the time of his 35th birthday.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the onset of weakness in the modern episode.

claims.statement: He had repeated head injuries, including concussions, during his playing career.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as history; the modern episode records a history of concussions without assuming any effect.

claims.statement: He was examined at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, from June 13 to June 19, 1939, and on his 36th birthday his internist, Harold C. Habein, certified the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; the clinic's statement added that he could continue in some executive activity.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern diagnosis; after the true-frame index date. The Hall of Fame spells the physician's name Hobein in one article.

source_links.locator: He could, however, continue in some executive activity

claims.statement: He retired from baseball on July 4, 1939, when the Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day before nearly 42,000 fans; in his speech he said that he considered himself "the luckiest man on the face of the earth."
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; after the true-frame index date.

claims.statement: In October 1939 he accepted Mayor La Guardia's appointment to a ten-year term as a New York City Parole Commissioner, was sworn in on January 2, 1940, and resigned quietly about a month before his death because his condition made the work impossible.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern work-accommodation theme (a desk role in public service); after the true-frame index date.

claims.statement: He died at his home on Delafield Avenue in the Fieldston section of the Bronx on June 2, 1941, at 37.

Researchers at the Boston University center for the study of traumatic encephalopathy have suggested that repetitive head trauma can cause a syndrome that mimics ALS, and that his repeated head injuries may have contributed to his decline; the Mayo Clinic has sealed his records, and it is not known whether an autopsy was performed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective hypothesis; the documented diagnosis remains ALS and the modern episode does not adopt the hypothesis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 35-year-old professional baseball player with a year of progressive weakness and loss of coordination: recognizing mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs, excluding mimics (MRI of the brain and cervical spine, blood tests, EMG and nerve conduction studies), and making the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis on the Gold Coast and revised El Escorial criteria; riluzole with liver test monitoring, genetic testing (tofersen only for an SOD1 variant) and edaravone discussed; a multidisciplinary ALS clinic tracking ALSFRS-R, forced vital capacity and weight; nutrition, speech and swallowing, mobility equipment, noninvasive ventilation thresholds, work accommodation, mood screening, and early advance care planning, on the AAN ALS practice parameters (1922).

problems.display: Progressive weakness and loss of coordination for about a year: fumbling with buttons and a bat, tripping on curbs, a fall on the ice in the winter, muscle cramps and twitching in the arms and thighs; no numbness, pain, double vision, or trouble speaking or swallowing. Examination: wasting of the hand muscles (left more than right), fasciculations in both arms and thighs, weakness of grip and of left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and a positive Hoffmann sign, normal sensation. Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs; evaluation for motor neuron disease and its mimics begun, with neuromuscular neurology consultation booked

hpi.narrative: Mr. Gehrig returns two weeks after his first visit and is seen the same day by Dr. Nakamura of neuromuscular neurology, who performed EMG and nerve conduction studies this morning. The MRI of the brain and cervical spine a week ago was normal. Since the first visit he has had no new symptoms but feels his grip is a little weaker; he has kept to walking and stretching and has not played or lifted. He has no trouble speaking, swallowing or breathing. He asked to hear the results himself first, and plainly.

assessment_plan.assessment: EMG shows active denervation (fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves) with chronic reinnervation and fasciculation potentials in the cervical, thoracic paraspinal and lumbosacral regions; motor responses are reduced in the hands with no conduction block, and sensory responses are normal. The MRI excludes cord compression and a structural lesion; calcium, vitamin B12, TSH and A1c are normal, the protein electrophoresis shows no monoclonal protein, the HIV test is negative, and the creatine kinase of 412 U/L fits denervation. With progressive weakness and upper and lower motor neuron signs in more than one region, this meets the Gold Coast criteria and is clinically probable ALS on the revised El Escorial criteria. ALSFRS-R 42 of 48; seated FVC 4.52 L (88% of predicted); maximal inspiratory pressure -86 cmH2O; a brief cognitive screen is normal. Dr. Nakamura gave him the diagnosis in person with Dr. Hollister present
plan: Riluzole 50 mg twice daily; ALT monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months
Genetic testing with genetic counseling today
Edaravone discussed; he chose to start with riluzole alone and revisit it
Multidisciplinary ALS clinic every 2 to 3 months, first full clinic visit in about five weeks
Breathing tests, weight and ALSFRS-R at every visit

hpi.narrative: Mr. Gehrig returns six weeks after the diagnosis, a week after his first full visit to the multidisciplinary ALS clinic, where he saw the physical, occupational and speech therapists, the dietitian, the respiratory therapist and the social worker. He has taken riluzole twice daily; he had mild nausea in the first week, which settled. The genetic panel found no disease-causing variant in SOD1, C9orf72, FUS, TARDBP or the other genes tested. His grip is weaker and he has tripped twice without falling; the clinic measured him for a left ankle-foot orthosis. He has decided to stop playing professionally and plans to say so publicly soon, and he is thinking about work he could do at a desk. He has been sleeping poorly and feels low at times but enjoys time with friends.

referral.question: Progressive weakness and loss of coordination over about a year in a 35-year-old professional baseball player, with hand wasting, widespread fasciculations, weakness of grip and left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and Hoffmann signs, and normal sensation. I am concerned about a motor neuron disease. Please evaluate with EMG and nerve conduction studies, exclude treatable mimics, and advise on diagnosis and care
referral.pertinent_history: About a year of gradually worsening weakness and clumsiness: a fall in his batting and fielding through last season, fumbling with buttons and the bat, tripping on curbs, a fall on the ice last winter, and cramps and twitching in the arms and thighs. Two days ago he took himself out of the lineup. No numbness, neck pain, double vision, ptosis, or trouble speaking, swallowing or breathing. Several concussions over his career, the last more than five years ago. Never smoked; one or two beers on some weekends. No medicines; no known allergies. Results today: blood count, sodium, potassium, creatinine, glucose and calcium normal; creatine kinase 412 U/L; vitamin B12 512 pg/mL; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; A1c 5.2%; ALT 32 U/L; seated FVC 4.62 L (90% of predicted). Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and an HIV test sent; MRI of the brain and cervical spine booked for next week. He wants results given to him first, plainly
questions: Does he have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or a treatable mimic such as cervical myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, or an inflammatory or metabolic myopathy?
What do the EMG and nerve conduction studies show, and which diagnostic criteria are met?
What disease-modifying treatment do you advise, and should genetic testing be done?
How should breathing, nutrition, speech and swallowing, and mobility be monitored, and when should we intervene?
How should we support his work, his mood and early planning for future care?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Gehrig, a 35-year-old professional baseball player, is seen at the request of Dr. Hollister for about a year of progressive weakness and loss of coordination, beginning with a decline in his play and progressing to fumbling with buttons, tripping on curbs and a fall on the ice, with cramps and twitching. He stopped playing two weeks ago. He has no sensory symptoms, neck pain, eye symptoms, or trouble speaking, swallowing or breathing. He has had several concussions in his career without lasting symptoms. No family history of ALS or dementia is known to him
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Hollister's intake note. MRI of the brain and cervical spine last week: normal, with no cord compression or structural lesion. Calcium 9.4 mg/dL, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.6 mIU/L, A1c 5.2%, creatine kinase 412 U/L; serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation shows no monoclonal protein; HIV test negative. Seated FVC 4.62 L (90%) at intake. EMG and nerve conduction studies this morning: normal sensory responses; reduced motor amplitudes in the median and ulnar nerves with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, fasciculation potentials and large, unstable motor units in the cervical (biceps, first dorsal interosseous), thoracic paraspinal, and lumbosacral (tibialis anterior, vastus lateralis) regions; bulbar muscles not yet affected

exam.finding: Wasting of the first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles, left more than right; fasciculations in both arms, thighs and calves; grip and finger abduction 4/5 on the right and 4-/5 on the left; left ankle dorsiflexion 4-/5

Speech and tongue normal; no facial weakness

assessment.assessment: Progressive motor weakness over about a year with upper and lower motor neuron signs in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, and EMG evidence of active and chronic denervation in three regions with normal sensory conduction and no conduction block. Cervical myelopathy and structural lesions are excluded by MRI; multifocal motor neuropathy by the absence of conduction block and the upper motor neuron signs; myopathy by the EMG pattern and the modest creatine kinase; and metabolic, paraproteinemic and infectious mimics by the blood tests. This meets the Gold Coast criteria and the revised El Escorial category of clinically probable ALS. ALSFRS-R 42 and FVC 88% of predicted. His past concussions do not change the diagnosis or treatment

recommendations: Diagnosis of ALS given to him in person today, with time for questions and written information
Riluzole 50 mg twice daily, with ALT monthly for 3 months and then every 3 months
Genetic testing for ALS-associated genes with genetic counseling today; tofersen only if an SOD1 variant is found
Edaravone discussed as an option with modest evidence in a selected group of patients; he chose to begin with riluzole alone and revisit it
Multidisciplinary ALS clinic every 2 to 3 months: ALSFRS-R, seated FVC and maximal inspiratory pressure, weight and swallowing at every visit; cognitive and behavioral screening; PHQ-9

Noninvasive ventilation when FVC falls below 50% of predicted, maximal inspiratory pressure is weaker than -60 cmH2O, overnight oximetry shows desaturation, or orthopnea appears; supine FVC and overnight oximetry when values fall
